title.title: Infinity-harmonic functions are $C^{1,\alpha}$ in every dimension
title.subtitle: Claim: for every $d \ge 3$, bounded infinity-harmonic functions have Hölder continuous gradients inside the ball

plain: The 'stretch as little as possible' way to fill in a surface: is its slope continuous in 3 or more dimensions?

beats.text: Aronsson's infinity-harmonic example, sliced along the $x_1$-axis
Its gradient is only $|x_1|^{1/3}$ near 0, which caps the Hölder exponent at $1/3$
Claim: in every $d \ge 3$ the gradient is Hölder with some $\alpha_d > 0$

steps: Suppose the gradient fails to settle at a power rate
Rescaling then gives a non-affine solution on all of space
A new Liouville theorem says none exists: contradiction

achievement.label: Gradient regularity of infinity-harmonic functions, d at least 3
achievement.context: Before: $C^{1,\alpha}$ in the plane (Evans–Savin 2008); in $d \ge 3$ only differentiability (Evans–Smart 2011)
achievement.note: $\alpha_d$ is not explicit; the optimal $1/3$ is not claimed

verify.detail: No Lean. The newest paper in the group (4 Oct 2026), so likely the least vetted
verify.ourCheck: We reviewed the paper; we did not check its Liouville theorem

voice.text: Aronsson's example, sliced along one axis. Its gradient behaves like a cube root near zero.
A failure would rescale into a solution that a Liouville theorem forbids.
Claimed: Hölder gradients in every dimension, three up.

sources.quote: Evans–Savin (Calc. Var. 2008): C^{1,α} in the plane; Evans–Smart (2011): everywhere differentiability in all dimensions.
Aronsson's example caps the exponent at $1/3$.
dated 4 Oct 2026, the most recent in the chunk, so likely the least vetted
α_d is non-explicit (compactness argument); no boundary or endpoint (α=1/3) claim.
